rv.q: Onscreen, Christopher Walken's oft-imitated shtick has veered into self-parody in recent years. But seeing it live is a whole other matter: On the evidence of his brilliant performance in Martin McDonagh's new play, 'A Behanding in Spokane,' the actor should have returned to the stage a long time ago.
Christopher Walken is your main man.

But especially coming after last season's brilliant revival of "The Cripple of Inishmaan," with its balance of searing poignancy and cruelty, the grubby razzle-dazzle of this funny throwaway feels a tad lazy.
His use of his signature arsenal of stylistic oddities has seldom been more enthralling.
Yet Berger fails to make audiences care much about his characters.
Mr. McDonagh has written a play that is more interested in shock than character, and while it contains some genuinely funny moments, it never quite coheres into a satisfying whole.
And it's as perfect a frisson as it always was meant to be - except for one problem.
But the play is on cruise control, and not even Walken can save it.
Toby’s characterization is as offensive as the language used to describe him.
McDonagh has basically written a noirish farce in which just about every available element of the threadbare set — the closet, the radiator, the suitcase — plays a significant role in the story.
But ultimately, A Behanding in Spokane feels as if McDonagh wrote it with one hand tied behind his back.
While hardly McDonagh's most fully realized effort, it leaves us wondering where his own singular imagination will take him next.
While I can't exactly say it's a bad play, it's just not a play at all.
Showcased at his spookiest best as a one-handed weirdo, Walken is hilarious and the sharply-staged comedy-thriller he haunts packs 90 minutes of nasty entertainment.
Though it offers many laughs and even a suitcase full of severed hands, "Behanding" is surprisingly undeveloped, unedited and lacking in dramatic tension.

cn.t: McDonagh's dark comedy receives mixed reviews, with critics praising Walken's magnetic performance but finding the play itself a slight, overextended sketch that lacks the depth of his previous work.
